blocks.prompt: The Crown That Falls Off
blocks.text: A deer's antlers are not horns. Horns stay on an animal for its whole life. Antlers do not. Every spring, a deer grows a new set. The antlers push up from its head. They are covered in soft skin called velvet. The velvet feeds the growing bone. By fall the antlers are hard, and the deer rubs the velvet off on a tree. In winter the antlers fall off. Then the deer grows a whole new set. It does this again every year.

blocks.prompt: The Crown That Grows Back
blocks.text: Horns and antlers are not the same thing. A goat's horns are made of the same stuff as your fingernails, and they stay on its head for life. Antlers are different. Antlers are bone, and a deer grows a fresh pair every single year. The growing starts in spring. Two soft bumps push out of the deer's skull and stretch upward. While they grow, they are wrapped in a furry skin called velvet. The velvet is full of blood vessels, and it carries food to the bone underneath. Antlers grow faster than any other bone in any animal. A big elk can add close to an inch a day. By fall, the bone has hardened and the velvet dries up. The deer scrapes it off against a tree trunk. Then, in late winter, something surprising happens. The antlers loosen and drop right off in the snow. The deer feels nothing. In spring, it starts all over again.

blocks.prompt: The Only Bone That Comes Back
blocks.text: Every mammal on Earth has the same problem: lose a body part, and it is gone. Cut yourself and you get a scar. Break a bone badly enough and it may never be the same. There is one exception, and it happens every year on the head of a deer. A deer's antlers are true bone, grown from two permanent bumps on the skull called pedicles. They are not horns. Horns are a sheath of keratin, the material in your fingernails, wrapped over a bony core, and they stay put for life. Antlers are grown and thrown away on a schedule. The trigger is daylight. As spring days stretch longer, a deer's body starts building. The antlers rise under a coat of fuzzy skin called velvet, which is threaded with blood vessels and nerves and delivers minerals to the bone forming underneath. The pace is extraordinary. Antler is the fastest growing bone known in any animal, and a bull elk in midsummer can add nearly an inch a day. That speed costs something. Building a heavy rack takes more calcium and phosphorus than a deer can eat, so its body borrows the difference from its own skeleton, thinning its ribs to thicken its crown, then repaying the loan later. By fall, growth stops, the bone hardens, and the velvet dries and is rubbed away on saplings. The antlers do their work through the mating season. Then, in late winter, they simply fall off. Mice and squirrels gnaw the fallen antlers for calcium, which is why the woods are not littered with them. And the deer begins again.

blocks.prompt: The Bone That Comes Back Every Year
blocks.text: Human medicine has a hard limit. We can set a broken bone and stitch a wound, but we cannot regrow what is lost. A severed finger does not come back. Among mammals there is exactly one organ that regenerates completely, on schedule, year after year, and it belongs to a deer. Antlers are often confused with horns, and the difference matters. A horn is permanent: a core of bone wrapped in a sheath of keratin, the same protein as your fingernails, and it grows slowly outward for the animal's whole life. An antler is temporary. It is pure bone, grown from a pedicle, a permanent knob on the skull, and it is discarded and rebuilt annually. Light runs the schedule. Lengthening spring days shift a deer's hormones, and construction begins. The antler rises beneath velvet, a living skin dense with blood vessels and nerves that ferries minerals to the bone forming below. Nothing else in the animal kingdom builds bone this quickly. A bull elk in full growth can lay down close to an inch of antler a day, assembling forty pounds of bone in a single summer. The bill comes due in calcium and phosphorus. A deer cannot eat enough to cover it, so it takes out a loan against itself, withdrawing minerals from its own ribs and skeleton to finish the rack, then rebuilding its skeleton afterward. For a few weeks, one of the healthiest animals in the forest is walking around with thinning bones. As daylight shortens, growth halts, the antler hardens into dead bone, and the velvet dries and is scraped off on saplings. The rack serves through the fall mating season, when males shove and spar and size each other up. Then hormones fall away, a thin layer of cells at the pedicle dissolves, and the antlers drop into the snow. The deer does not notice. Mice, squirrels, and porcupines find the sheds and gnaw them down for calcium, which is why a forest floor is not carpeted in antlers. Not every deer follows the rule. Reindeer are the one species whose females grow antlers too, and they keep theirs through winter after the males have dropped theirs. The Chinese water deer skips antlers altogether and fights with long curved tusks instead. But the pattern holds: build a crown, use it, throw it away, build it again. Laboratories study the pedicle closely, because whatever instructions it follows, the rest of us appear to have lost them.

blocks.prompt: The Crown That Costs a Skeleton
blocks.text: Consider a problem in engineering. You must build a branched structure of solid bone, up to four feet across and forty pounds in weight, on top of a skull. You must finish it in about four months, using an animal that eats leaves. Then you must throw the whole thing away and do it again next year, and the year after that, for a decade. No mammal on Earth solves this problem except the deer, and it solves it every spring. Start with what an antler is not. It is not a horn. A horn is a permanent core of bone sheathed in keratin, the protein in your fingernails, and it grows outward in slow layers for life. Cattle, goats, and antelope wear horns. An antler is naked bone, and it is disposable. It erupts from a pedicle, a permanent bony pillar on the skull, and everything above that pillar is temporary. Daylight starts the clock. As spring days lengthen, melatonin falls, testosterone shifts, and stem cells resting in the pedicle begin to divide. What follows is the fastest bone growth known in any animal. A bull elk in midsummer lays down close to an inch of antler a day, sheathed in velvet, a living skin so dense with blood vessels and nerves that you can feel a pulse in it. The velvet is not decoration. It is the supply line. The cost is brutal and specific. A rack demands more calcium and phosphorus than a browsing animal can possibly eat in a season, so the deer withdraws the shortfall from its own skeleton. Its ribs thin. Its bones weaken. For several weeks each summer, a healthy deer is walking through the woods in a state that in a human would be diagnosed as osteoporosis, and then it quietly rebuilds itself once the antler is done. The crown is paid for out of the frame that carries it. When growth stops, the bone dies and hardens, the velvet withers, and the deer scrapes it away against saplings. Through the fall rut, the antlers do the job they were built for. They are weapons, but more often they are arguments. A rack is an honest advertisement: it cannot be faked, because only a well fed, healthy, mature animal can afford to grow a large one. Most contests are settled by looking. Then the hormones drop, specialized cells eat away a thin seam at the top of the pedicle, and the antlers fall off, often without the deer breaking stride. Mice, squirrels, and porcupines gnaw the sheds to powder for their calcium. The forest floor is not carpeted in antlers because the forest eats them. There is one more twist, and it is the reason cancer researchers read deer papers. Antler growth is uncontrolled cell division on an enormous scale, which is more or less the definition of a tumor. Genetic work on deer has found that the genes driving antler growth include ones that cause cancer in other mammals, and that deer carry extra copies of tumor suppressor genes running alongside them. Deer grow a fast, wild, enormous mass of tissue every year and then stop it on command, cleanly, without it turning into a tumor. Nothing else does that. So the deer stands at the intersection of three questions humans cannot answer: how to regrow a lost organ, how to build bone at speed, and how to let cells divide furiously and then tell them to quit. It has been answering all three, on the same schedule, since long before anyone was watching.
